type: classifying — about the economy; also quality in the *profitable* sense
position: both — mostly before a noun (*economic growth*); after *be* to name the kind of problem (*The reasons were economic*) and in the *profitable* sense (*It isn't economic to repair it*)
comparison: not gradable — in the *economy* sense; *more economic* occurs only in the *profitable* sense
contrast: *economic* is about the economy; *economical* is about spending little. Test: if you can say *cheap to run* or *saves money*, use *economical*: *an economical car* (экономичный автомобиль), not *an economic car*. *economic growth*, *an economic crisis* (экономический кризис), never *an economical crisis*. Russian *экономический* = *economic*; *экономичный* and *экономный* = *economical*. The *profitable* sense (*It isn't economic to fix it*) is the one place the two come close. Russian *экономика* is two English nouns: *the economy* (экономика страны) and *economics* (экономика как наука). Both first syllables are heard in American speech: ek-uh- and ee-kuh-.

senses.gloss: Relating to the economy of a country or region — trade, industry, jobs and money — or to economics as a subject.
examples: The country is going through a period of slow *economic* growth.
Many families left the town for *economic* reasons.
Their problems are *economic*, not political.

senses.gloss: Making enough money to be worth doing; profitable — mostly in business and energy writing.
examples: The mine closed because it was no longer *economic* to run.
At today's prices, it isn't *economic* to repair an old TV.
Solar power is getting *more economic* every year.

position: both — *an economical car*, *The car is economical*
takes: *with* + noun = using little of (*economical with words*); *it's economical to* + verb
contrast: See *economic*. *economical* never means *about the economy*: *economic policy*, not *economical policy*; *economic reforms* (экономические реформы), not *economical reforms*. In everyday American speech people often say *cheap to run* or *fuel-efficient* about machines and *thrifty* or *careful with money* about people. *economical with the truth* (не договаривающий, лукавящий) is a polite, originally British way to say someone is lying by leaving things out.

senses.gloss: Cheap to use or run, because it uses little money, fuel or other resources.
examples: Small cars are usually *more economical* to run.
Buying rice in bulk is the *most economical* way to shop.
The new furnace is quiet and *economical*.

senses.gloss: Of a person: careful not to spend or waste money.
examples: My grandmother was an *economical* cook who wasted nothing.
We have to be *economical* until I find a new job.

senses.gloss: Using no more words, movements or effort than are needed.
examples: He writes in a clean, *economical* style.
The pitcher has a smooth, *economical* delivery.
Her essay is short and *economical*: every sentence does a job.

position: both — mostly before a noun (*a historic day*); after *be* too (*This moment is historic*)
contrast: *historic* = important in history, or famous for its past: *a historic victory* (историческая победа), *a historic building*. *historical* = about the past or the study of it: *historical records* (исторические документы), *a historical novel* (исторический роман). Test: if you can say *famous* or *memorable*, use *historic*; if you can say *from the past* or *about the past*, use *historical*. *a historical event* simply happened; *a historic event* changed things. Russian *исторический* covers both, so decide each time. Americans say *a historic* with the h pronounced; *an historic* sounds old-fashioned or British. In *historic lows* and *historic times* the two words overlap, and both are used.

senses.gloss: Important in history, or likely to be remembered as important.
examples: The two leaders signed a *historic* peace agreement.
It was a *historic* day for the city when the team finally won.
Fans called it the *most historic* game they had ever seen.

senses.gloss: Old and interesting because of its past, and worth preserving.
examples: We stayed at a *historic* inn built in 1790.
The *historic* district is full of brick row houses.
Charleston is famous for its *historic* homes.

senses.gloss: Of a level or amount: the highest or lowest ever recorded.
examples: Mortgage rates fell to *historic* lows that spring.
Home prices reached *historic* highs last year.

senses.gloss: Belonging to the time of written history, as opposed to prehistoric times — mostly in *historic times*.
examples: The lake has never dried up in *historic* times.
Only two volcanoes in the region have erupted in *historic* times.

position: both — almost always before a noun (*historical records*); after *be* mainly in the *really existed* sense (*Is the story historical or made up?*)
contrast: See *historic*. *historical* is the neutral word for anything connected with the past or with history as a subject; it never means *famous* or *memorable*: *a historic moment* (исторический момент), not *a historical moment*. *historical* before *data*, *prices* or *trends* just means *from past years*. Russian *исторический* covers both words.

senses.gloss: Relating to history or the study of history; about the past.
examples: The museum has a large collection of *historical* documents.
She's doing *historical* research on the Civil War.
The town's *historical* society runs tours every Saturday.

senses.gloss: Of a book, movie or painting: telling a story set in the past.
examples: My mom loves *historical* novels set in the Old West.
The show is a *historical* drama about the first English settlers.

senses.gloss: Really having lived or happened in the past, not only in stories.
examples: Scholars still argue about whether King Arthur was a *historical* figure.
The movie mixes *historical* fact with fiction.
Is the story *historical*, or did the author make it up?

senses.gloss: Based on figures from past years, as opposed to current ones.
examples: *Historical* data shows that prices rise every December.
The model predicts sales from *historical* trends.

position: both — mostly before a noun (*a classic mistake*); after *be* in the *style* and informal senses (*Her look is classic*, *That's classic!*)
contrast: *classic* = excellent and lasting, typical, or traditional in style: *a classic movie*, *a classic mistake* (типичная ошибка), *a classic suit*. *classical* = of ancient Greece and Rome, of serious Western music, or of an old established system: *classical architecture*, *classical music* (классическая музыка), *classical ballet*. Test: if you can say *typical* or *great and lasting*, use *classic*; if you can say *ancient* or *traditional art form*, use *classical*. *classic music* is a mistake for *classical music*, and *a classical example* for *a classic example*. Russian *классический* covers both. *a classic* (a great book or movie) and *the classics* (Greek and Latin literature) are nouns.

senses.gloss: Of the highest quality and admired for a long time; one of the best of its kind.
examples: It's a *classic* American novel that every teenager reads.
The band played all their *classic* hits.
We watched a *classic* Hitchcock movie last night.

senses.gloss: Very typical; a perfect example of its kind.
examples: Forgetting to back up your files is a *classic* mistake.
He showed all the *classic* signs of a heart attack.
It's a *classic* case of too little, too late.

senses.gloss: Simple and traditional in style, so it does not go out of fashion.
examples: You can't go wrong with a *classic* white shirt.
Her style is *more classic* than her sister's.

senses.gloss: Of cars, music or TV shows: from an earlier period and still loved today.
examples: He spends every weekend restoring *classic* cars.
The station plays *classic* rock all day.
We grew up watching *classic* cartoons on Saturday mornings.

senses.gloss: Informal: very funny, or exactly what you would expect of someone.
senses.ru: в своём репертуаре; ну это классика (разг.)
examples: He fell asleep at his own party? That's *classic*.
Showing up an hour late is *classic* Mike.

position: both — almost always before a noun (*classical music*); after *be* mostly in the *style* sense (*The lines of the building are classical*)
comparison: not gradable — except in the *style* sense: *more classical*
contrast: See *classic*. *classical music* covers everything from Bach to modern concert music, not only the Classical period of Haydn and Mozart. *classical* never means *typical*: *a classic example*, not *a classical example*. Nor does it mean *old and still loved* about cars or rock: *classic cars*, *classic rock*.

senses.gloss: Relating to ancient Greece and Rome, their languages, art and ideas.
examples: She studied *classical* Greek and Latin in college.
The Capitol is built in the *classical* style, with tall columns.
Many *classical* writers told stories about the gods of Olympus.

senses.gloss: Of music: in the serious Western tradition of composers like Bach and Beethoven, not pop, rock or jazz.
examples: He listens to *classical* music while he works.
She trained as a *classical* pianist.
The *classical* station plays Mozart every morning.

senses.gloss: Traditional and long established, as opposed to newer or modern forms.
examples: She trained in *classical* ballet before switching to jazz dance.
*Classical* physics can't explain how atoms behave.
Modern Arabic grew out of *Classical* Arabic.

senses.gloss: Simple, balanced and elegant, like the art of ancient Greece.
examples: The actress was known for her *classical* beauty.
The new library is *more classical* in design than the old one.

position: both — before a noun or after *be* in the *powered by electricity* sense (*an electric stove*, *Is the stove gas or electric?*); mostly after a verb in the *exciting* sense (*The mood was electric*)
comparison: not gradable — except in the *exciting* sense: *more electric*, *most electric*
contrast: *electric* is for a thing that runs on electricity or carries it: *an electric toothbrush*, *an electric shock*. *electrical* is the general word for electricity as a system, a subject or a kind of fault: *electrical wiring*, *an electrical engineer*, *an electrical fire*. Test: name one machine and use *electric*; name a category, a job or a problem and use *electrical*. Many phrases take only one: *electric guitar*, *electric chair*; *electrical engineering*, *electrical storm*. Only *electric* has the *exciting* sense. Americans say *the electric bill* and *the electric company*, where British English says *the electricity bill*. Neither is *electronic* (электронный: using chips, as in *electronic devices*). Russian *электрик* (the worker) is *electrician*; the color *электрик* is *electric blue*.

senses.gloss: Working by electricity, or carrying or producing it.
examples: We just bought an *electric* car.
The dog got a shock from the *electric* fence.
Is your stove gas or *electric*?

senses.gloss: Relating to the supply of electricity to homes and businesses.
examples: Our *electric* bill doubled in July.
The *electric* company shut off their power.

senses.gloss: Full of excitement and energy; thrilling.
examples: The atmosphere in the stadium was *electric*.
The crowd was even *more electric* in the second half.
She gave an *electric* performance on opening night.

senses.gloss: Of a color: very bright and strong.
examples: She wore an *electric* blue dress to the prom.
The walls were painted an *electric* green.

position: both — almost always before a noun (*electrical wiring*); after *be* to name the kind of fault (*The problem is electrical*)
contrast: See *electric*. *electrical* usually names a category (*electrical equipment*) or a field (*electrical engineering*); *electric* names the machine (*an electric heater*). *an electrical heater* is not wrong, but *an electric heater* is what people say, and *electrical engineering* is fixed: never *electric engineering*. *electrical* has no *exciting* sense: *an electric atmosphere*, not *an electrical atmosphere*.

senses.gloss: Using, carrying or involving electricity; relating to electricity in general.
examples: Unplug all *electrical* appliances before you leave.
An *electrical* fire started in the basement.
The problem with the car turned out to be *electrical*.

senses.gloss: Relating to the science of electricity or to work with it as a job.
examples: He has a degree in *electrical* engineering.
Hire a licensed *electrical* contractor to move the outlet.

position: attributive only — *on alternate days*, *an alternate route*
contrast: Pronunciation: the adjective is AWL-tur-nuht; the verb *to alternate* is AWL-tur-nayt. Only *alternate* means *every other*: *on alternate days* (через день). Only *alternative* means *unconventional*: *alternative medicine*, *alternative rock*, never *alternate medicine*. For *another choice* American English uses both: *an alternate route* and *an alternative route*; some editors and British readers accept only *alternative*, so prefer it in formal writing. *an alternate* is also a noun: a substitute juror, delegate or player. Russian *альтернативный* is usually *alternative*; *через день* is *every other day* or *on alternate days*.

senses.gloss: Available as another choice, in place of the usual or planned one.
examples: Take an *alternate* route if the bridge is closed.
We need an *alternate* plan in case it rains.
The judge replaced the sick juror with an *alternate* juror.

senses.gloss: Happening on every second day, week or other unit; every other.
examples: The class meets on *alternate* Tuesdays.
The kids spend *alternate* weekends with their dad.
Write your answers on *alternate* lines.

senses.gloss: Of two things: coming one after the other, again and again.
examples: Arrange *alternate* layers of pasta and cheese in the dish.
The flag has *alternate* red and white stripes.

senses.gloss: Existing as another version of events or of the world.
examples: The show is set in an *alternate* universe where dinosaurs never died out.
She writes *alternate* history novels.

position: both — almost always before a noun (*an alternative plan*); after a verb only in the informal *unconventional* sense (*Her taste in music is pretty alternative*)
comparison: not gradable — except in the informal *unconventional* sense: *more alternative*
contrast: See *alternate*. The noun *an alternative* (вариант, выбор) is more common than the adjective: *There's no alternative*, *an alternative to surgery*; the *to* belongs to the noun. *alternative* never means *every other*: *on alternate days*, not *on alternative days*. The stress is on the second syllable: awl-TUR-nuh-tiv.

senses.gloss: Available as another choice; able to be used instead of something else.
examples: If the flight is canceled, the airline will book you on an *alternative* flight.
We need to find an *alternative* way to pay for the project.
Police posted *alternative* routes around the parade.

senses.gloss: Different from what is usual or traditional, and often chosen as a rejection of it.
examples: More patients are trying *alternative* medicine like acupuncture.
She listened to *alternative* rock in high school.
Her taste in music is pretty *alternative*.

senses.gloss: Of energy or fuel: not coming from oil, coal or natural gas.
examples: The state is investing in *alternative* energy such as wind and solar.
City buses run on *alternative* fuels.

position: both — *a childish remark*, *Don't be childish*
form: -ish from *child* — like a child, in a bad way
contrast: *childish* criticizes: an older person acting like a small child (ребячество). *childlike* praises or describes: the good qualities of a child, such as trust and wonder (детская непосредственность). Test: *Don't be childish* is a reproach; *childlike wonder* is a compliment. Neither is the word for things made for children: Russian *детские книги* is *children's books*, *детская одежда* is *kids' clothes*, *детская площадка* is *a playground*.

senses.gloss: Of an older person or their behavior: silly and immature, like a small child.
examples: Stop being so *childish* and apologize to your sister.
It was a *childish* thing to do.
The argument got *more childish* by the minute.

senses.gloss: Typical of a child or of childhood.
examples: The note was written in big, *childish* handwriting.
We could hear *childish* voices coming from the yard.

position: both — *childlike wonder*, *Her voice sounded childlike*
contrast: See *childish*. *childlike* is usually positive or neutral; *childish* is negative. Said about an adult's mind or judgment, *childlike* can sound patronizing (*a childlike understanding of money*), so use it with care.

senses.gloss: Having the good qualities of a child, such as innocence, trust and enthusiasm.
examples: My grandfather never lost his *childlike* sense of wonder.
She has an almost *childlike* trust in people.
He was *more childlike* than any of the kids he taught.

senses.gloss: Looking, sounding or moving like a child.
examples: The robot has a *childlike* face with big round eyes.
She spoke in a soft, *childlike* voice.

position: attributive only — *continual delays*; after *be* it sounds odd, so use *constant*: *The noise was constant*
contrast: *continual* = happening again and again, with breaks: *continual phone calls* (звонки один за другим). *continuous* = without any break: *continuous rain* (непрерывный дождь). Test: a dripping faucet is *continual*; a running faucet is *continuous*. Careful writers keep this line; in general use *continual* also covers *without stopping* (sense 2), and *constant* covers both. Only *continuous* works for space (*a continuous line*) and grammar (*the present continuous*). Russian *постоянный* is most often *constant*.

senses.gloss: Happening again and again, often in an annoying way.
examples: I'm tired of your *continual* complaining.
The project suffered from *continual* delays.
*Continual* interruptions made it impossible to work.

senses.gloss: Going on for a long time without stopping.
examples: He lived in *continual* pain after the accident.
The city was under *continual* attack for three months.

position: both — *continuous rain*, *The noise was continuous*
contrast: See *continual*. *continuous* never means *repeated with breaks*: *continual interruptions*, not *continuous interruptions*, unless there was no pause at all. In grammar, American textbooks usually say *progressive* (*the present progressive*) where British ones say *continuous*; both mean the *be* + *-ing* form.

senses.gloss: Going on without a pause or break.
examples: Patients in the ICU need *continuous* monitoring.
The noise from the highway is *continuous*, day and night.
The company is committed to *continuous* improvement.

senses.gloss: Without gaps in space; forming an unbroken line or surface.
examples: Draw one *continuous* line without lifting your pen.
A *continuous* fence runs along the highway.

senses.gloss: In grammar: formed with *be* + *-ing* to show an action in progress; progressive.
examples: *I am reading* is in the present *continuous*.
The past *continuous* describes what was happening at a moment in the past.

position: both — *an efficient system*, *The system is efficient*
contrast: *efficient* = doing something without wasting time, money or energy; *effective* = getting the result you want. Test: a medicine that cures you is *effective*; a factory that makes more cars with less power is *efficient*. A thing can be one without the other: a sledgehammer is an *effective* way to crack a nut, but not an *efficient* one. Russian *эффективный* covers both, so ask whether you mean *it works* (*effective*) or *it works without waste* (*efficient*).

senses.gloss: Working well without wasting time, money or energy.
examples: LED bulbs are much *more efficient* than old light bulbs.
We need an *efficient* way to handle all these orders.
The new trains are fast and *efficient*.

senses.gloss: Of a person: organized and able to get work done quickly and well.
examples: Our office manager is incredibly *efficient*.
An *efficient* waiter kept our glasses full all night.

ru: эффективный, действенный; фактический; вступающий в силу
position: both — *an effective drug*, *The drug is effective*; before a noun only in the *actual* sense (*in effective control*); after *be*, or opening a phrase, in the *starting* sense (*effective immediately*)
takes: *in* or *at* + *-ing* (*effective in reducing pain*); *against* + disease or pest (*effective against the flu*); *for* + a problem (*effective for back pain*); in the *starting* sense *as of* + date, or a bare date (*effective May 1*)
contrast: See *efficient*: *effective* is about the result, *efficient* about the waste. Russian *эффектный* (showy, striking) is usually *striking*, *impressive* or *eye-catching*: *an eye-catching dress* (эффектное платье); *effective* in that sense (sense 2) is limited to how something works in a design or a picture. *effective immediately*, *effective May 1*, with no *from*, is the usual American way to give a start date. The adverb *effectively* often means *in effect*, *actually*: *He effectively ran the company*.

senses.gloss: Producing the result that is wanted; working well.
examples: Exercise is one of the *most effective* ways to reduce stress.
The vaccine is highly *effective* against the virus.
She's a very *effective* teacher.

senses.gloss: Making a strong and pleasing impression; striking.
examples: The red door looks very *effective* against the gray brick.
The dark walls make an *effective* background for the paintings.

senses.gloss: Real in practice, though not in name or on paper.
examples: The general was the *effective* ruler of the country.
Rebels are in *effective* control of the north.
After deductions, their *effective* tax rate was 12 percent.

senses.gloss: Officially in use or in force, starting from a stated time.
examples: The new rules are *effective* as of January 1.
She resigned, *effective* immediately.
The price increase becomes *effective* next month.

position: both — *an imaginary friend*, *The danger was imaginary*
contrast: *imaginary* = not real: *an imaginary enemy* (воображаемый враг). *imaginative* = good at imagining, creative: *an imaginative writer* (писатель с богатым воображением). Test: an *imaginary* story isn't true; an *imaginative* story is original. *imaginable* = possible to imagine, and it often follows its noun or a superlative: *every color imaginable*, *the worst thing imaginable*. Russian *мнимый* in the sense *supposed* can be *imaginary* (*an imaginary threat*), but *мнимый друг* is *a false friend*.

senses.gloss: Existing only in the mind; not real.
examples: Our daughter had an *imaginary* friend named Blue.
The equator is an *imaginary* line around the earth.
His illness was *imaginary*, but his fear was real.

senses.gloss: In math, of a number: a real number multiplied by the square root of minus one.
examples: An *imaginary* number squared gives a negative result.
Every complex number has a real part and an *imaginary* part.

position: both — *an imaginative child*, *The design is imaginative*
contrast: See *imaginary*. *imaginative* praises a mind or a piece of work; it never means *not real*: *an imaginary friend*, not *an imaginative friend* (that would be a creative friend).

senses.gloss: Of a person: good at thinking of new and interesting ideas; creative.
examples: She's the *most imaginative* kid in her class.
We need an *imaginative* designer for this project.

senses.gloss: Of an idea, plan or piece of work: new, clever and original.
examples: The school came up with an *imaginative* solution to the parking problem.
The movie's special effects are wildly *imaginative*.
It's an *imaginative* retelling of an old fairy tale.

senses.gloss: Relating to the imagination, or done by using it.
examples: Blocks and dolls encourage *imaginative* play.
It takes an *imaginative* leap to picture the city in 1850.

position: both — usually after a verb (*barely comprehensible*); before a noun less often (*in comprehensible English*)
contrast: *comprehensible* = possible to understand: *a comprehensible explanation* (понятное объяснение). Don't confuse it with *comprehensive* = covering everything: *comprehensive insurance* (полное страхование), *a comprehensive study* (всестороннее исследование). Test: *comprehensible* asks whether you can understand it; *comprehensive* asks whether anything is left out. In everyday speech Americans say *understandable* or *easy to understand*. *understandable* also means *forgivable* (*His anger is understandable* — вполне понятно, простительно); *comprehensible* never does.

senses.gloss: Able to be understood.
examples: The manual is barely *comprehensible* to anyone without a tech background.
She explained the new tax law in clear, *comprehensible* English.
His speech became *more comprehensible* once he slowed down.

position: both — *a respectful silence*, *Be respectful*
takes: *of* + noun (*respectful of their privacy*); *to* or *toward* + person (*respectful toward her elders*)
contrast: *respectful* describes how you treat others: you show respect (уважительный, почтительный). *respectable* describes how others see you: you deserve respect, or you are socially acceptable (порядочный, приличный). Test: a *respectful* student is polite to the teacher; a *respectable* student has a good reputation. *respective* (соответствующий) is a third word: *They went back to their respective homes*.

senses.gloss: Showing respect and politeness toward someone or something.
examples: The crowd stood in *respectful* silence during the anthem.
Please be *respectful* of your neighbors and keep the noise down.
He's been *more respectful* toward his teachers this year.

position: both — *a respectable family*, *He looked respectable*
contrast: See *respectful*. Russian *респектабельный* suggests money and an expensive look; English *respectable* means *proper* or *good enough*, not rich: *a respectable neighborhood* is safe and decent, not necessarily wealthy. For the expensive look say *upscale* or *high-end*. *a respectable score* is good, not great.

senses.gloss: Considered by society to be good, proper or correct.
examples: She came from a *respectable* family in Boston.
He had a steady, *respectable* job at the bank.
They wanted to move to a *more respectable* neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Good enough in appearance to be seen in public.
examples: Put on something *respectable* — we're having dinner with your grandparents.
I need a *respectable* suit for the interview.

senses.gloss: Fairly good or fairly large; good enough.
examples: The team finished the season with a *respectable* 9-7 record.
She earns a *respectable* salary.
Their first album sold a *respectable* 50,000 copies.

senses.gloss: Deserving respect, or deserving to be taken seriously.
examples: There are *respectable* arguments on both sides.
He was a *respectable* scholar, widely cited in his field.

position: both — mostly before a noun (*industrial waste*); after *be* about places and style (*The area is mostly industrial*)
comparison: not gradable — except about places and style: *more industrial*
contrast: *industrial* = about industry: *an industrial town* (промышленный город). *industrious* = hardworking: *an industrious student* (трудолюбивый студент). Test: machines, waste and places are *industrial*; people are *industrious*. British *industrial action* (a strike or slowdown) is not used in the US: Americans say *a strike* or *a work stoppage*; American *labor relations* is British *industrial relations*. Russian *индустриальный* and *промышленный* are both *industrial*.

senses.gloss: Relating to industry and the making of goods in factories.
examples: *Industrial* waste was dumped in the river for decades.
He was badly hurt in an *industrial* accident.
*Industrial* production rose 2 percent last month.

senses.gloss: Of a place: having a lot of factories and industry.
examples: Pittsburgh grew into a major *industrial* city.
The company moved to an *industrial* park outside town.
The east side of the river is *more industrial* than the west.

senses.gloss: Made for use in factories or businesses, not at home; very strong.
examples: The restaurant has an *industrial* dishwasher.
You'll need an *industrial*-strength cleaner for that stain.

senses.gloss: In a style that copies old factories, with bare brick, metal and concrete.
examples: The coffee shop has an *industrial* look, with exposed pipes and steel beams.
They bought a downtown loft with an *industrial* feel.

position: both — *an industrious student*, *She's very industrious*
form: -ous from *industry* in its old meaning, *hard work*
contrast: See *industrial*. *industrious* is a formal, written word; in conversation Americans say *hardworking*. It never describes factories or cities: *an industrial city*, not *an industrious city*, unless you mean its people work hard.

senses.gloss: Working hard and steadily.
examples: The *industrious* students stayed after class to finish their projects.
Ants are famous for being *industrious*.
She's the *most industrious* person on the team.

position: both — *an uninterested look*, *He seemed uninterested*
comparison: more/most — *more uninterested*, *most uninterested*; *less interested* often sounds more natural
contrast: *uninterested* = not interested, bored (безразличный). *disinterested* = having nothing to gain, fair (беспристрастный): *a disinterested judge*. Test: an *uninterested* referee isn't watching the game; a *disinterested* referee doesn't care who wins. Many Americans say *disinterested* for *uninterested*, and teachers and editors often mark it wrong, so keep them apart in writing. In speech the natural phrase is *not interested*: *I'm not interested*. Don't confuse *uninterested* (a person who feels no interest) with *uninteresting* (a thing that causes none — скучный). Russian *незаинтересованный* can mean either: *незаинтересованная сторона* is *a disinterested party*.

senses.gloss: Not interested; not wanting to know about something or take part in it.
examples: My son is completely *uninterested* in sports.
The cat gave the new toy an *uninterested* look.
The longer the lecture went on, the *more uninterested* the students looked.

position: both — *a disinterested observer*, *Her advice was disinterested*
takes: *in* + noun or *-ing* — only in the *not interested* sense (*disinterested in school*)
form: dis- + *interested*, where *interest* means a personal stake
contrast: See *uninterested*. The *impartial* sense is the one careful writers keep and the one tests check; the *not interested* sense is old and widespread, but a reader may think you've made a mistake. With *in* after it, *disinterested* can only mean *not interested*. Russian *бескорыстный* about a person who helps for nothing is usually *selfless* or *unselfish*: *a selfless volunteer*.

senses.gloss: Not influenced by any personal advantage; fair and impartial.
examples: We need a *disinterested* third party to settle the dispute.
Her advice was completely *disinterested* — she had nothing to gain.
The panel wanted the *most disinterested* experts it could find.

senses.gloss: Not interested; showing no interest — common in speech, but many editors call it a mistake for *uninterested*.
examples: The kids looked totally *disinterested* in the museum tour.
He seemed *disinterested* in anything I had to say.

position: both — *compulsory voting*, *Attendance is compulsory*
contrast: *compulsory* = required by a rule (обязательный). *compulsive* = unable to stop yourself (навязчивый): *a compulsive gambler*. Test: laws, courses and exams are *compulsory*; habits and people are *compulsive*. In American English *compulsory* sounds formal or foreign; the everyday words are *required* (*a required course*) and *mandatory* (*a mandatory evacuation*, *mandatory drug testing*). Russian *обязательный* about a person means *reliable* or *dependable*: *a reliable employee* (обязательный сотрудник), never *a compulsory employee*. *Обязательно приходи!* is *Be sure to come!*

senses.gloss: Required by a law or a rule; that must be done.
examples: School attendance is *compulsory* for children in every state.
Some countries have *compulsory* voting.
Gym class was *compulsory* at my high school.

position: both — *a compulsive liar*, *His shopping became compulsive*
contrast: See *compulsory*. Before a person noun, *compulsive* means the habit controls the person: *a compulsive shopper* (шопоголик), *a compulsive liar* (патологический лжец). *obsessive-compulsive* is the medical term (OCD). British reviewers call a gripping show *compulsive viewing*; Americans usually say *addictive* or *binge-worthy*. Russian *компульсивный* is a clinical word; English *compulsive* is common in everyday talk.

senses.gloss: Of behavior: caused by a strong urge that is hard or impossible to control.
examples: She struggled with *compulsive* eating for years.
His hand-washing became *more compulsive* over time.
Checking your phone every few minutes can become *compulsive*.

senses.gloss: Of a person: unable to stop doing something, usually something bad.
examples: He's a *compulsive* liar.
Her father was a *compulsive* gambler who lost the family house.

position: both — *a healthy baby*, *The baby is healthy*
contrast: *healthy* is the everyday American word for both *not sick* and *good for you*: *healthy kids*, *healthy food*. *healthful* means only *good for you* and sounds formal; some teachers say food must be *healthful*, not *healthy*, but *healthy food* is standard. Test: a person can be *healthy* but never *healthful*. Russian *здоровый* meaning *big* or *strong* (*здоровый парень*) is *big* or *hefty*, not *healthy*: *a big guy*. Before nouns about medicine use the noun *health*: *health insurance*, *health care*, *a health problem*, not *healthy insurance*.

senses.gloss: Physically or mentally well; not sick.
examples: The baby was born *healthy* and strong.
She's the *healthiest* she's been in years.
Regular checkups keep your pets *healthy*.

senses.gloss: Good for your health.
examples: Try to eat a *healthy* breakfast every morning.
Walking to work is *healthier* than driving.
They're trying to live a *healthy* lifestyle.

senses.gloss: Showing that someone is in good health.
examples: Her skin has a *healthy* glow.
The boy has a *healthy* appetite.

senses.gloss: Of a business, an economy or a relationship: strong and working well.
examples: The company is in *healthy* financial shape.
They have a *healthy* marriage.
The economy is *healthier* than it was a year ago.

senses.gloss: Normal and sensible; showing good judgment.
examples: Swimmers should have a *healthy* respect for the ocean.
A little *healthy* competition is good for the team.
Keep a *healthy* skepticism about online reviews.

senses.gloss: Fairly large.
examples: The team built a *healthy* lead in the first half.
They sold the house for a *healthy* profit.

position: both — *a healthful diet*, *The food is healthful*
contrast: See *healthy*. *healthful* appears in food labels, health articles and government guidelines: *a healthful diet*. It never describes a person's condition: *a healthy child*, not *a healthful child*.

senses.gloss: Good for your health.
examples: The school cafeteria now serves *more healthful* meals.
People once moved to Arizona for its dry, *healthful* climate.
The report lists the *most healthful* snacks for kids.

position: both — *a definite answer*, *Nothing is definite yet*
takes: *about* + noun, *-ing* or *wh*-clause — in the *sure* sense (*She was definite about the date*)
contrast: *definite* = clear and fixed: *a definite plan* (конкретный план). *definitive* = final and authoritative, the last word on something: *the definitive book on jazz* (лучшая, исчерпывающая книга о джазе). Test: *definite* answers *Is it certain?*; *definitive* answers *Is this the final, best version?* Don't use *definitive* just to sound formal: *a definite yes*, not *a definitive yes*. Russian *определённый* meaning *a certain* is not *definite*: *to a certain extent* (в определённой степени), *a certain kind of person*. Spelling: *definite*, never *definate*.

senses.gloss: Fixed, clear and not likely to change.
examples: We don't have a *definite* date for the wedding yet.
Nothing is *definite* until we sign the contract.
I need a *more definite* answer by Friday.

senses.gloss: Clearly seen, felt or noticed; real.
examples: There's been a *definite* improvement in his grades.
Speaking Spanish is a *definite* advantage in this job.
There's a *definite* chill in the air tonight.

senses.gloss: Of a person: sure and firm about something.
examples: She was very *definite* about not wanting to move.
He wasn't *definite* about when he'd be back.

senses.gloss: In grammar: showing that a noun refers to something already known — in *the definite article*.
examples: *The* is the *definite* article in English.
Russian has no *definite* article.

position: both — *a definitive answer*, *The results were definitive*
contrast: See *definite*. *definitive* is formal and strong; *definite* is the everyday word. *a definite answer* is simply clear; *a definitive answer* settles the question for good. Russian *дефинитивный* is rare; think *окончательный* or *эталонный*.

senses.gloss: Final and settling a question, so that it cannot be doubted or changed.
examples: The DNA test gave a *definitive* answer.
The Supreme Court's ruling was *definitive*.
We need *more definitive* evidence before we act.

senses.gloss: The most complete and reliable of its kind, so that it becomes the standard.
examples: It's considered the *definitive* biography of Lincoln.
This is the *definitive* guide to the national parks.
Critics call it the *definitive* recording of the song.

position: both — *an exhaustive search*, *The list is not exhaustive*
contrast: *exhaustive* = complete, leaving nothing out (исчерпывающий). *exhausting* = making you very tired (утомительный, изнурительный): *an exhausting day*. *exhausted* = very tired (измученный): *I'm exhausted*. Test: an *exhaustive* search looks everywhere; an *exhausting* search wears you out. *comprehensive* is the close synonym and is more common for coverage: *a comprehensive plan*. Russian *исчерпывающий ответ* in conversation is usually *a complete answer* or *a full answer*; *exhaustive* belongs to searches, lists, studies and reviews.

senses.gloss: Including every possible detail or possibility; very thorough.
examples: Police carried out an *exhaustive* search of the woods.
This list is not *exhaustive* — it's just a starting point.
The second study was even *more exhaustive* than the first.
